title: Temples of the diaspora
hook: immigrant temples as homes far from home

segments.voice: Yesterday, chaplains and volunteers sitting with the gilana, the sick, in hospices and prisons. Your line: in hard places. Did you pull up a chair for someone? Today closes a week. Day one thousand fifty.

This week walked through some hard and hopeful ground: the debate over women's ordination, trust broken and faced, mindfulness in offices, monks in labs, robes on trees, chairs pulled up to hospice beds. Now a quieter scene. A house on an ordinary street, in a city far from Asia. Shoes are piled by the front door. Inside, the living room has become a shrine room, and the kitchen smells of rice and curry. Children in the back room are learning letters their grandparents grew up with. Today, the temples people built when they moved far from home.
screen: `A WEEK OF HARD AND HOPEFUL GROUND.` → `SHOES PILED BY THE DOOR.` → `A HOUSE BECOMES A TEMPLE.`

segments.voice: When families from Sri Lanka, Thailand, Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia, Tibet, Korea, Japan and elsewhere settled in new countries, some of them built temples, often starting small. A rented room. A house. A building that used to be something else. Sometimes a monk was invited from home to live there. And the temple quickly became more than a place to sit. It's where a festival is kept on the right moon. Where a child learns the chants and the old language. Where a newborn is blessed, a wedding is honored, and a funeral is held in a way that feels right. Where a newcomer finds someone who knows how to fill out the forms. The Sigalovada Sutta lays out what a lay follower and the renunciants he supports, monks among them, owe each other, in paraphrase: lay people keep their doors open and offer what renunciants need; renunciants teach, steer people from harm, and show the way. In a diaspora temple, that old exchange is easy to see. The community feeds the monk, and the monk helps hold the community together. These temples also carry real strains. Children grow up speaking a different language than their elders. Some temples offer one service in the old language and a meditation class in English, and the two groups don't always meet. Some communities are working on that, and some aren't yet. An old line in the Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, fits these places: "trust is the best of relationships." A temple far from home runs on trust, and it builds it too.
screen: `A RENTED ROOM, A HOUSE, A MONK INVITED.` · `MORE THAN A PLACE TO SIT.` · `DOORS OPEN, THE WAY SHOWN.` · then, large: `TRUST IS THE BEST OF RELATIONSHIPS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: welcome someone new. Sit, and let the breath settle. Remember a time you were the new one: a new school, a new job, a new country, a new street. Who made it a little easier? What did they do? Let the memory stay a moment. Then bring to mind someone new near you now: a neighbor who just moved in, a new coworker, a family at your children's school. Picture one small welcome you could give them. A name learned. A tip about the town. A plate of food. The bell holds the time.
Vihara. A dwelling, and so a temple, built by people who moved far from home, where the chants, the festivals, the old language and the community are kept alive. Today's word.
Your line: a home far from home. Today, learn the name of one person who's new around you, and use it the next time you see them. Day one thousand fifty.

howItsDone: Some Buddhist communities who have moved abroad have built temples, from rented rooms to large buildings, where they keep festivals, teach children the chants and language, support resident monastics and welcome newcomers.

original.note: Pali vihara: a dwelling, and so a monastery or temple, a place to live as much as to sit.

trapdoor: what you thought: a temple abroad is a building for prayers.
what it means: a home far from home, where festivals, language, food and family milestones are kept.
what a scholar hears: the Sigalovada Sutta's duties between lay people and monks, lived out in a new country.

notes: Dhammapada 204 in Max Müller: 'Health is the greatest of gifts, contentment the best riches; trust is the best of relationships, Nirvana the highest happiness.' Only the third clause is quoted; confirm wording.
The Sigalovada Sutta's reciprocal duties (DN 31) are compressed; the sutta lists five ways lay people serve ascetics and six ways ascetics respond. Confirm the paraphrase.
The list of origin countries is illustrative; confirm it reads fairly and isn't taken as exhaustive.
The generational and convert/immigrant strain is described gently and without ranking. Confirm framing with a Keeper from a diaspora community.
Week-end look-back in the hook names days 1044–1049.

Editor pass: 'many of them built temples', 'many temples begin', 'what do many families do' and 'often build' softened to 'some' (claims rule); 'old bargain' changed to 'old exchange' to avoid a transactional framing; 'let the memory warm a moment' smoothed.

Audit pass: DN 31 speaks of samanas and brahmins (renunciants in general), not Buddhist monks only; the teach now says 'renunciants, monks among them'. Rest checked: Dhp 204 Müller wording, week-end recap of days 1044–1049; sound.
